issue.body:
### What happened?

`iree-run-module` throws an [`OUT_OF_RANGE` error](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/blob/main/runtime/src/iree/modules/hal/module.c#L1037-L1038) when executing the training step for models which train more than ~32 variables. For example, when attempting to execute training for a model with 36 variables the following error is thrown:

```
iree/runtime/src/iree/modules/hal/module.c:1038:
  OUT_OF_RANGE; count 37 of iree_hal_fence > 32; while invoking native function hal.fence.join; while calling import;
```

Merely updating more than ~32 variables is insufficient so I've included the whole training step in the reproducer. The count above also doesn't solely depend on the number of variables.

### Steps to reproduce your issue

The error above can be reproduced using the following reproducer: [`out_of_range.mlir`](https://gist.github.com/phoenix-meadowlark/ba0f76235510dc3c01ff0e5aba7d0f94)

```shell
iree-compile \
  --iree-hal-target-backends=vmvx \
  --iree-input-type=mhlo \
  /tmp/out_of_range.mlir \
  -o /tmp/out_of_range.vmfb

iree-run-module \
  --device=local-sync \
  --entry_function=train_step \
  --function_input=100x16000xi16 \
  --function_input=100x16000xf32 \
  --function_input=100xi16 \
  --module_file=/tmp/out_of_range.vmfb
```

```
EXEC @train_step
iree/runtime/src/iree/modules/hal/module.c:1038: OUT_OF_RANGE; count 37 of iree_hal_fence > 32; while invoking native function hal.fence.join; while calling import;
[ 1]   native hal.fence.join:0 -
[ 0] bytecode hotword.train_step:4038 [
  ]
      at /tmp/out_of_range.mlir:75:14
      at /tmp/out_of_range.mlir:38:3; invoking function 'train_step'
```

### What component(s) does this issue relate to?

Runtime

### Version information

cfedd317979496241f4db26343f358b9f1845879

### Additional context

_No response_

issue.body:
In addition to the linalg fusion we do today there's another level of fusion we could be performing that combines entire dispatch regions. This can happen just based on the `flow.dispatch.workgroups` op and using the `flow.dispatch.tensor` interface.

Conceptually each dispatch region is just a function called at runtime - the call of which may be happen on a thread pool, GPU command processor, etc. The benefit of having these calls modeled in Flow/HAL is that if the execution engine can execute the work in parallel (same call on may execution units) or concurrently (overlapping with other calls) we reap those benefits. There are cases where this cannot happen, though, and we have those encoded in the flow IR use-def chains.

As an example, this is a great separation of work:
```mlir
// these two run concurrently and are each parallelized:
%0 = flow.dispatch.workgroups[1024, 1, 1](%arg0)
%1 = flow.dispatch.workgroups[1024, 512, 1](%arg1)
// this reduces the inputs and runs after both complete, but uses far fewer workgroups to do so:
%2 = flow.dispatch.workgroups[8, 1, 1](%0, %1)
```

While this is not:
```mlir
// each runs sequentially:
%0 = flow.dispatch.workgroups[1, 1, 1](%arg0)
%1 = flow.dispatch.workgroups[1, 1, 1](%1)
%2 = flow.dispatch.workgroups[1, 1, 1](%2)
```

In the second case we are getting no benefits from the separation and only incurring overhead: we are paying the cost of encoding and performing multiple calls, round-tripping the results/arguments through memory, and requiring additional transient memory.

The aspirational case here is https://www.shadertoy.com/view/wsByWV (which I will bring up til the end of time :) - that could be done in 400 dispatches or like it is here 4 with loops, conditionals, etc. We (as something executing functions) aren't restricted to what linalg can model in a single loop nest but only what data traversal hazards we have. It's all just code :)

We should be able to identify some of these cases where the separation is pessimizing performance and fix them up by folding consumers up into producers. Conceptually it's like identifying mergable dispatches, creating a new dispatch, and inlining both dispatch regions into it. The `flow.dispatch.tensor` arguments can be elided through and the rest of the code outside of the dispatches gets its use-def chains patched up. Being able to safely do this is one of the reasons we require tensors at this level.

There are gotchas, like if the work is parallelized it may be doing things that prevent workgroups from running within the same dispatch (such as a scatter followed by a gather). We should be able to identify this by either adding traversal information to the flow ops (similar and derived from how linalg has parallel/reduce/etc tags) or inspecting the `flow.dispatch.tensor` load and store ops. To start, even just combining dispatches that are all 1x1x1 would help in the situations where we can't or don't want to detensor and are performing very thin sequences of sequential work.

The major work is this cost modeling (of which to start could just be "is possible?"), and there may be some cleanup work or generalization required lower into the codegen stack if there are any lingering assumptions from back in the old pipeline around whether there is a single root linalg loop/etc. The pass to perform this work where it is possible, though, is likely just a hundred lines or so of replacing ops, using mlir::inlineRegion, and removing unneeded args/results (which in theory is handled by the closure optimizations already on the dispatch region op).

This will improve raw performance (less memory round-tripping), latency (less command processor round-tripping), memory utilization (fewer materialized transient buffers), and code size (less code needed to setup buffers/dispatch unique entry points). It may harm deduplication but that's a cost we can balance (and we need better solutions than "bitwise identical" for deduplication anyway).

issue.body:
This removes unused args/results, inlines uniformly constant args/results, and deduplicates the ones that remain. This is similar to the block patterns we have and designed to be run in a fixed-point iteration so that cse/canonicalization/block patterns can all help each other.

In the future this should be extended to support globals by biasing towards making loads/stores local with uses. Today we'll end up with a lot of global loads -> call -> global stores and that's blocking the naive global folding/fusion pass from kicking in. We'll probably want a dialect/op interface like the inliner has to control this (and may be able to just reuse the inliner interface).

timeline.body:
I've made progress here and have the fence issue fixed - I've got to write tests tomorrow but you can check it out here while I do that: #10911.

I'm getting assertion failures in CPU codegen doing an arith::CmpIOp folder on vector types. That's terrifying but unrelated. I suspect you're running a release compiler build with assertions disabled otherwise you'd have hit that long before you hit runtime issues :)

btw just remembered you can use `--mlir-print-debuginfo=false` to hide all those source location lines from your errors if they're making things tricky for you.

issue.body:
With the input in #10903 and #10911 applied I hit an assertion triggered by `arith::CmpIOp::fold`; it looks like the folder (and potentially many others) are not handling all types and this IR causes it to die:

```mlir
      %9 = arith.extsi %7 : vector<4xi16> to vector<4xi32>
      %cst_3 = arith.constant dense<0> : vector<4xi32>
      %11 = arith.cmpi slt, %9, %cst_3 : vector<4xi32>
```

here where it's doing an unconditional cast to IntegerType:
https://github.com/iree-org/iree-llvm-fork/blob/ec89299aff0bf2ed39caa544dfa55316e3d02efa/mlir/lib/Dialect/Arith/IR/ArithOps.cpp#L1456-L1462

There's a large number of `cast<IntegerType>()` and such in that file and it'd be good to verify that arith is intended to be used with vector types and if it is then probably filing upstream bugs to make it work. My hope is that this is just because of the `m_Zero` pattern match returning true for element attrs whereas many of the other matchers are checking for specific attr types and that this would be easy to scrub.

Source:
```mlir

  %workgroup_count_x = hal.interface.workgroup.count[0] : index
  %2 = affine.apply affine_map<()[s0] -> (s0 * 100)>()[%workgroup_id_x]
  %3 = affine.apply affine_map<()[s0] -> (s0 * 100)>()[%workgroup_count_x]
  scf.for %arg0 = %2 to %c100 step %3 {
    %4 = flow.dispatch.tensor.load %1, offsets = [%arg0], sizes = [100], strides = [1] : !flow.dispatch.tensor<writeonly:100xi32> -> tensor<100xi32>
    %5 = flow.dispatch.tensor.load %0, offsets = [%arg0], sizes = [100], strides = [1] : !flow.dispatch.tensor<readonly:100xi16> -> tensor<100xi16>
    %6 = scf.for %arg1 = %c0 to %c100 step %c4 iter_args(%arg2 = %4) -> (tensor<100xi32>) {
      %extracted_slice = tensor.extract_slice %5[%arg1] [4] [1] : tensor<100xi16> to tensor<4xi16>
      %extracted_slice_0 = tensor.extract_slice %arg2[%arg1] [4] [1] : tensor<100xi32> to tensor<4xi32>
      %c0_1 = arith.constant 0 : index
      %c0_i16 = arith.constant 0 : i16
      %7 = vector.transfer_read %extracted_slice[%c0_1], %c0_i16 : tensor<4xi16>, vector<4xi16>
      %c0_i32_2 = arith.constant 0 : i32
      %8 = vector.transfer_read %extracted_slice_0[%c0_1], %c0_i32_2 : tensor<4xi32>, vector<4xi32>
      %9 = arith.extsi %7 : vector<4xi16> to vector<4xi32>
      %cst = arith.constant dense<12> : vector<4xi32>
      %10 = arith.addi %9, %cst : vector<4xi32>
      %cst_3 = arith.constant dense<0> : vector<4xi32>
      %11 = arith.cmpi slt, %9, %cst_3 : vector<4xi32>

Interesting - I wonder why you don't hit the same assert I am in #10915 - may be worth trying one time in Debug just to make sure the IREE_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS flag is working as it should (I only run in Debug).

Hmmm, I did a `Debug` build from scratch with `IREE_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS` unset and I'm not hitting any asserts when I compile [`out_of_range.mlir`](https://gist.github.com/phoenix-meadowlark/ba0f76235510dc3c01ff0e5aba7d0f94).

In both configurations trying to execute the VMVX-compiled module causes `iree-run-module` to hang after printing `EXEC @train_step`. I actually noticed this behavior for some other modules as well, but wasn't sure if it was a bug or VMVX just being incredibly slow for some reason.
VMVX is incredibly slow - try llvm-cpu :)
Gotcha! Training with llvm-cpu is currently blocked by https://github.com/iree-org/iree/issues/10839 so I switched to VMVX to see if I could find any other issues that might pop up down the line.
Oh nice - that's a duplicate of the issue I was hitting - we should make sure @MaheshRavishankar / @hanhanW / someone codegen sees it!
